title: Apartment Marketing for Property Managers: A Weekly Checklist in Under an Hour
seoTitle: Weekly Apartment Marketing Checklist for Property Managers
seoDescription: A weekly marketing checklist for community managers and leasing teams: what to check on Google, reviews, social and your website in under an hour.
excerpt: A community manager does not need a marketing department to keep a property visible. One focused hour a week on Google, reviews, social and the website covers most of what renters see.
imageAlt: Wooden clipboard with lined paper reading TO DO in handwritten marker, on an orange background
imageIdea: Real photo of a leasing office desk with a printed weekly checklist on a clipboard and a laptop beside it, daylight, no screen content or names visible.
author: Michael Shad, Founder of The SocialDM
bodyHtml:
Once a week, a community manager can cover the marketing that matters most in under an hour: confirm your Google Business Profile facts, reply to new reviews, check that specials and availability match everywhere, look at one social post and test the website on a phone. The goal is not to create more content. It is to make sure what renters already see is accurate.

I wrote this for the person who runs the property and also owns its marketing. Pick a day, put it on the calendar, and work through the list in order.

What does the whole checklist look like?

Six checks, about 50 minutes in total. The times are what I would budget for a single stabilized community with a normal week of reviews.

CheckWhat to look atTime
1. Google Business ProfileHours, phone, website link, special hours, photos from the public10 minutes
2. ReviewsReply to every new review, escalate anything sensitive15 minutes
3. Specials and pricingSame offer on website, Business Profile and listing sites10 minutes
4. Website on a phonePhone number, tour link, application link, floor plan prices5 minutes
5. SocialOne useful post, comments and messages answered5 minutes
6. NotesWrite down what changed and what needs help5 minutes

What should you check on Google each week?

Search your community name on your phone and read your Business Profile the way a renter would. Confirm the hours, phone number, website link and address, and look at any new photos the public added.

Google's local ranking page says complete and accurate information helps Google match your business to the right searches. Wrong office hours are the most common error I see, so check holidays and short closures ahead of time. Google's special hours help page suggests confirming hours for official holidays even when they match your regular hours, so renters can see the listing is accurate.

If something on the profile was changed and you did not change it, fix it and note it. A weekly look is how you catch unexpected changes before renters do. If the profile looks right but renters still are not finding you on Maps, see why apartments lose tours in Google Maps.

How should the team handle reviews in a weekly routine?

Reply to every new review, positive or negative, and send anything about safety, fees, deposits, discrimination or legal threats to your regional manager before replying. Do this weekly at minimum, and daily if review volume is high.

Google says more reviews and positive ratings can help local ranking, and that replying shows you value feedback. For example replies to common situations, use our guide on how to respond to apartment reviews.

When you ask residents for reviews, ask everyone, not only happy residents, and never tie a reward to what the review says. Google's content policy treats incentives for reviews and selectively asking for positive reviews as fake engagement. The FTC's final rule on fake reviews also bans offering incentives conditioned on a review expressing a particular sentiment. When in doubt, ask without offering anything.

How do you make sure specials and prices match everywhere?

Pick your current special and check that the same offer, dates and fine print appear on your website, your Business Profile post and each listing site you pay for. Mismatched specials are one of the fastest ways to lose trust before a tour.

Check starting prices on the floor plan pages at the same time. If your revenue management system changes prices daily, make sure the website pulls them correctly and that no page still shows last month's offer. Remove expired Business Profile posts and replace them with the current one.

What should you check on the website?

Open your website on a phone and try to do what a renter would do: call, schedule a tour and start an application. If any of those take more than a few taps or fail, that is the most important fix of the week.

  • Call button: tap it and make sure it reaches the leasing office or the right call center.
  • Tour scheduling: pick a time and confirm the request arrives where the team will see it.
  • Floor plans: prices and availability load, and the plan names match your listings.
  • Pet and fee details: written on the page, not only inside a PDF.

How much social media is enough?

For most communities, one useful post a week and same day replies to comments and messages is enough. A resident event, a new amenity, a finished renovation or a neighborhood spot renters care about will do more than a generic holiday graphic.

Spend the rest of the five minutes reading comments and direct messages. A prospect asking about pets in a comment is a lead, and an unanswered question is visible to everyone who comes after.

What should you write down at the end?

Write three lines: what you fixed, what you could not fix, and anything that changed in the market, such as a competitor's new special. Over a month, those notes show patterns that a dashboard will not.

Send the notes to your regional or marketing lead with the numbers you already track. Our post on multifamily marketing metrics that predict leases covers which numbers are worth adding. This weekly rhythm is also the backbone of LocalLift, where we track the Google, Maps and AI side for the team so the hour can go to fixes.

Questions we hear

How long should weekly apartment marketing take?

For one stabilized community, about an hour a week covers the essentials: Google Business Profile, reviews, specials, a website check on a phone and one social post.

What is the most important weekly marketing task for a property manager?

Making sure your Google Business Profile facts are right and replying to new reviews. Google says complete, accurate information helps match you to the right searches.

Can we offer residents a gift card for leaving a review?

Not tied to the review content. The FTC bans incentives conditioned on a particular sentiment, and Google treats incentives for reviews as fake engagement, so asking without a reward is the safest approach.

How often should a community post on social media?

One useful post a week is enough for most communities, as long as comments and messages get answered the same day.

Do we need to update holiday hours on Google if they do not change?

Google suggests confirming hours for official holidays even when they match your regular hours, so renters can see the listing is accurate.

takeaways: A community manager can cover the marketing renters see most in about an hour a week.
Check your Google Business Profile hours, phone, links and public photos every week, and confirm holiday hours ahead of time.
Reply to every new review, and never tie a reward to what a review says.
Test the call button, tour scheduling and application link on a phone each week.
